comparator.academicYear: 2026-2027 programme overview (Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences curriculum archive) for the Fall-2026 entrant cohort; programme and curriculum pages checked 2026-09-29
comparator.sourceNotes: Reconstructed from the official FASoS 'Bachelor Digital Society 2026-2027' programme overview (s3, linked from the curriculum archive s4), which lists every year-1 and year-2 course and skill with its EC and assessment and, for year 3, the regular components (Research Experimentation Zone 4 EC, Controversies in Digital Society 9 EC, Bachelor Thesis 17 EC) and 30 EC of elective units of study. Year 1 totals 60 EC (5 courses and 6 skills), year 2 totals 60 EC (5 courses and 5 skills) and year 3 totals 60 EC. The optional Mentor Scheme in year 3 carries 0 EC and is therefore not a component. The programme has no formal routes or tracks; the year-3 30 EC is open elective space (minor, study abroad, internship, literature exam or approved electives) and is preserved as a single open component rather than invented content. The programme page (s0), the curriculum page (s1) and the why-this-programme page (s2) confirm the interdisciplinary identity (technology, business, ethics, people and planet), the coding basics and the 'hint of data science', but the course-level Osiris catalogue was not accessible, so course content beyond titles, EC and assessment is known only from those pages. A BA degree, three years, English, full-time, Maastricht.

Genuine open elective space. The 2026-2027 programme overview lets each student compile 30 EC from a minor or interfaculty minor, a study abroad, an internship (max. 24 EC), a literature exam (max. 12 EC), electives offered by another FASoS bachelor, or approved electives outside the faculty; no single content is prescribed.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
Business & Economy in the Age of AI

core: Digital society as an interdisciplinary object of study: how digitalisation transforms culture, politics, the economy and the environment, introduced in What is (a) Digital Society?, Artificial Society and Controversies in Digital Society

Digital cultures, media and the history of ICT: Digital Cultures, Virtual Worlds and ICT Revolutions: Continuity and Change, covering influencers, virtual worlds, emerging media and the historical development of computing
Digital politics, regulation and rights: Digitalisation and Politics and Regulating the Digital, including how governments regulate technology and online safety, privacy and digital rights
Digital ethics: ethical analysis of data, algorithms and generative AI, taught through The 'Good Life' and the programme's ethical-dilemma focus
Digital technologies and critical making: Introduction to Digital Technologies I and II, Critical Making, the basics of coding and cyber security, and designing digital systems for social good

Research methods for digital society: What is Research?, Making Knowledge, Using Digital Sources, Quantitative Data Analysis, Working with Big Data, Qualitative Research Methods and Interdisciplinary Research Design, including data analysis for social questions
Independent research: the Research Experimentation Zone and the 17-EC Bachelor Thesis that concludes the programme
Digital economy, business and organisations: Social and Environmental Impacts of the Digital Economy and the study of digital business, leadership and innovation
Creative digital communication: creating with digital media and formats, from Virtual Worlds to the creative communication that the programme develops
adjacent: Elective and minor directions attached to the 30-EC open elective space: arts and heritage, European studies, gender and diversity, globalisation and development, great thinkers, sustainable healthcare, psychology, entrepreneurship, sustainability, art law and policy, human and legal decision-making and post-growth cities
Data, algorithms and AI as technical objects: the science behind generative AI, social-media algorithms and data analysis for social questions
Sustainable digital futures: how digital systems can be designed for environmental and social sustainability, linking technology, people and the planet, sustainability and post-growth society
questions: How do digital technologies, generative AI and social-media algorithms reshape society, behaviour, beliefs and politics, and how can they be used responsibly?
How can digital and technological systems be designed and governed so that they are environmentally and socially sustainable?

trace: introduces the study of film and media, tracing the historical development of cinema and the elements of film form (narrative, cinematography, editing, sound) and treating media as cultural forms that reflect and shape society; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's media and digital-culture analysis by supplying the analytical vocabulary, although its main object is film rather than digital media

studies how pre-digital media technologies such as cassette tapes, typewriters and printed books shaped the production, circulation and preservation of knowledge, through material analysis and historical interpretation; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's history-of-ICT component (ICT Revolutions: Continuity and Change) but addresses earlier media technologies rather than the digital revolution itself

examines how television, film, podcasts and TikTok narratives shape social attitudes and everyday life, treating viral moments as cultural snapshots of contemporary values and anxieties; it directly engages the social-media and digital-culture content of the target's Digital Cultures, although from an American mainstream-media perspective

analyses how film, photography, sound and digital media make ecological processes and environmental risk visible and shape how environmental problems are understood; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the link between media and the planet in the target's technology, people and planet identity

teaches data cleaning, manipulation and visualization for tabular, spatial and text data with hands-on examples from the sciences, social sciences and humanities, and ends in an own research project applying data analysis to a research question; it directly implements introductory data handling and analysis for social questions, the basis of the target's Working with Big Data and data-science content

teaches structured and object-oriented programming in Python with testing and debugging; it directly addresses the basics of coding that the programme page names for the target's Introduction to Digital Technologies I, although it is a computer-science gateway course rather than a digital-society course

examines the ethics of AI (fairness and bias, privacy, responsibility and accountability, the moral status of AI systems, existential risk and political implications) together with the psychology of AI; it directly implements the target's digital-ethics and generative-AI-and-society direction

teaches moral theories (virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism) and practical ethics topics such as poverty, future generations and climate change; it directly implements the ethical reasoning behind the target's The 'Good Life' and digital-ethics content, but treats ethics generally rather than technology ethics specifically

analyses political systems and democracies, including phenomena such as democratic backsliding, with the theory-driven qualitative and quantitative research tools of political science; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's Digitalisation and Politics by supplying political-science foundations, but has no digital content of its own

covers human-rights law (treaties, monitoring mechanisms, case law) and its historical and philosophical foundations; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's online safety, privacy and digital-rights direction, but treats rights generally rather than digital rights specifically

examines actors, institutions, decision-making rules and policy-making in the European Union; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's regulation and policy component (Regulating the Digital, digital politics and policy) by teaching how public authority turns interests into policy, but does not itself cover digital regulation

introduces the concepts, methods and theories of sociology for analysing societies from everyday interactions to long-standing institutions; it supplies the social-science foundation for the target's What is (a) Digital Society? and Artificial Society

engages contemporary social theory on civil society, the public and civil sphere, social capital and social trust (Habermas, Fraser, Alexander); it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's analysis of publics, trust and society under digitalisation, but does not address digital media directly

teaches the four stages of qualitative research (design and preparation, data collection and management, analysis and interpretation, dissemination); it directly implements the target's Qualitative Research Methods

teaches research design (operationalization, experimental design, sampling, surveys) and descriptive and inferential statistics including an introduction to multivariate statistics; it directly implements the research-methods foundation of the target's What is Research? and its quantitative skills
teaches multivariate statistical models (linear regression, factor analysis, ANOVA/ANCOVA, logistic regression); it directly implements the target's Quantitative Data Analysis

traces AI from early research to generative AI and analyses its business, economic and societal implications (competitiveness, labour markets, inequality, climate change) together with AI governance and ethics (bias, privacy, fairness, regulation); it directly implements the target's Social and Environmental Impacts of the Digital Economy and its digital-business direction

develops creative communication through experimental writing, sound and performance within critical reading and reflective writing; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's creative-communication direction, but its media are poetry, sound and performance rather than digital formats specifically

examines persuasion strategies (framing, nudging, cognitive shortcuts) in media, advertising, business and public discourse together with the ethics of persuasion; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's question of how social-media algorithms and digital media shape beliefs and behaviour, but is not specific to digital platforms

is a team research project on a problem posed by an external partner organisation, giving supervised applied interdisciplinary research experience; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's Interdisciplinary Research Design and applied research training, but its subject is sustainability rather than digital society

teaches predictive modelling (linear regression, classification, resampling, tree-based methods, support vector machines, clustering) with real-world applications; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's Working with Big Data by extending data analysis from description to prediction

trains recognition of misinformation, fake news and cognitive biases, with a historical overview of misinformation in politics and society; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's online-harms and information-literacy themes, but is not specific to digital platforms

teaches algorithm design and analysis with weekly laboratory work, experimental performance analysis and an account of how algorithms have shaped the modern world; it gives the technical understanding of algorithms behind the target's social-media-algorithm and AI content

teaches differentiation, integration, complex numbers and differential equations through applied projects; it is the formal prerequisite of the Neural Networks & Deep Learning and Probability & Statistics courses and supplies the mathematical foundation that the AI and statistics content builds on, a complementary rather than direct contribution to the concept

introduces relational database systems and SQL (relational theory, normalization, query processing, authorization); it makes a specific complementary contribution to data analysis for social questions by teaching how the data behind digital systems are stored, queried and protected

explains the architecture and protocols of the Internet and the structure of operating systems; it directly supplies the technical understanding of how digital networks work that underpins the target's Introduction to Digital Technologies II and online-safety content

builds and trains neural networks and applies them to computer vision, large language models and generative AI in Python; it directly implements the science behind generative AI named in the target's programme description

provides mathematical statistics (probability theory, distributions, sampling, parameter estimation, simulation); it directly implements the quantitative foundations of data analysis for social questions at a more theoretical level than the target itself

introduces planning and decision-making techniques for AI systems in deterministic and non-deterministic environments, addressing uncertainty, partial observability and optimizing behaviour under constraints; it directly implements the technical side of how algorithmic systems decide

examines what drives consumer behaviour and engagement, how customer trust can be built responsibly, and digital and AI-driven marketing; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the question of how algorithms and digital marketing shape behaviour

integrates psychology into economic theory, showing how biases, heuristics and framing shape decisions, with behavioural experiments; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the question of how choice environments and algorithms shape behaviour, but is not specific to digital settings

teaches search in complex and adversarial environments and optimization by rational agents; it directly implements a technical account of how AI agents choose actions, complementing the Decision-making in AI course

introduces sustainability through the planetary-boundaries model with the physics, materials-science and mathematical modelling tools needed for the environment and sustainability cluster; it supplies the foundation for the technology and planet strand and is the formal prerequisite of Sustainability Essentials II and Earth Observation

extends the sustainability foundation into waves, chemistry and materials science and how they relate to sustainability, with an individual journal and a project; it is the formal prerequisite of Renewable System Design and R3 and supplies the technical grounding for the technology and planet strand

covers the drivers of anthropogenic climate change (greenhouse gases, sea-level rise, ocean acidification, climate feedbacks) and the societal transformations it drives; it directly implements the environmental-limits side of the target's technology, people and planet identity

teaches life-cycle assessment of products, processes and services from raw-material extraction to disposal or re-use and strategic planning for a circular economy; it directly implements the methods for evaluating the environmental impact of technology and products in a sustainable-technology question

analyses sustainability through governance: how sustainability policies are made and enforced from local to international level, which actors are most influential and how public opinion and politics interact; it directly implements the governance of sustainable technology in the target's policy-oriented direction

teaches assessment of energy-use patterns and strategies for reducing consumption or moving to solar, wind and bioenergy solutions, with technical and economic analysis reported to a partner company; it makes a specific complementary contribution by giving the engineering and economic basis of low-carbon technology, without covering digital systems specifically

examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy, resource security and stewardship, with laboratory skills and inorganic chemistry; it makes a specific complementary contribution to sustainable technology through resource recovery and circularity

studies social-movement theories and environmental justice with case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas, integrating degrowth, anti-colonial and feminist perspectives and environmental peacebuilding; it directly implements the social and post-growth side of the sustainable-future strand

analyses how the climate crisis is communicated and contested in texts, films, exhibitions, protest art and social media, ending in a project in which students enter the debate; it directly implements communication for social and environmental goals in the sustainable-future strand

has teams develop a start-up concept from ideation to pitch using design thinking, market validation and business planning, including social entrepreneurship; it directly implements the entrepreneurship direction and is the formal prerequisite of Strategy & Digital Transformation and International Business & Governance

has students develop a strategic plan for responsible digital transformation, identify digital value opportunities and assess the impact of digital technologies on strategy, business models and social responsibility; it directly implements the target's digital business, leadership and innovation direction

examines cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade shaping international companies; it makes a specific complementary contribution to responsible business under globalisation in the sustainable-future strand

examines market failure, public goods, externalities, taxation and redistribution with theoretical models and empirical evidence; it makes a specific complementary contribution by providing the economic framework for sustainability policy and its distributional effects

introduces microeconomics (supply and demand, consumer behaviour, market structure) and macroeconomics (aggregate output, unemployment, inflation); it makes a specific complementary contribution as the economic foundation for the growth and post-growth debate in the sustainable-future strand

studies economic growth, national income, inflation and unemployment, fiscal and monetary policy, business cycles and crises over the short, medium and long run; it makes a specific complementary contribution by giving the growth analysis against which post-growth perspectives are assessed

studies biogeochemical processes, (waste)water treatment and engineered processes that recover valuable resources from waste and anthropogenic resource cycles; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the resource-recovery side of sustainable technology, complementing R3

gives hands-on GIS and geospatial-data experience with satellite and drone imagery to model and analyse human impacts on ecosystems and climate; it directly implements the use of digital data technologies for sustainability in the target's sustainable-digital-future direction

covers sustainable livestock farming, integrated pest management, sustainable supply chains, organic farming and precision agriculture; it makes a specific complementary contribution by showing how digital and precision technologies are applied to a sustainable food system, but is not itself a digital-systems course

alternatives.label: Closest match to Digital Society: Media, Society, Ethics and Data Skills
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum has seven courses on media, communication and misinformation (Introduction to Film & Media, Media Archaeology, From T.V. to TikTok, Media & the Environment, Persuasive Communication, Creative Communication Laboratory and Calling Bullshit), three on politics and law (Foundations of Comparative Politics, European Union Politics and Human Rights), three on sociology and social theory (Introduction to Sociology, New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory and Qualitative Research Methodology), two on ethics (Ethics and AI Ethics), four on data, programming and algorithms (Introduction to Data Science, Machine Learning, Introduction to Programming and Algorithms & Data Structures), two on quantitative research methods (Research Methods & Statistics and Statistics & Experimental Methods), one on the business and economy of AI, one applied research project and Personal & Professional Development. No single field dominates, so the label names the media, social, ethical and data strands, and 'closest match to Digital Society' makes clear that UCR has no digital-society degree curriculum and covers the target's territory through related disciplines.
alternatives.concept: The strongest defensible UCR response to the Bachelor Digital Society at Maastricht University, which studies digitalisation through sociological, ethical, technical, political and economic lenses and ends in independent research. The programme recreates that interdisciplinary mix from UCR's media and communication courses (digital cultures, media history, social media, persuasion, misinformation), politics, law and human-rights courses (regulation, policy and rights), sociology and social theory, ethics and AI ethics, business and economy of AI, and hands-on data science, programming and algorithms, with qualitative and quantitative research methods and one externally posed research project. It preserves genuine limitations: UCR offers no course on digital politics, virtual worlds, critical making or digital-society theory.
progression: Introductory courses precede the courses that build on them wherever the schedule allows: Introduction to Film & Media and Media Archaeology (semester 1) precede From T.V. to TikTok (semester 4) and Media & the Environment (semester 6); Introduction to Sociology (semester 1) precedes New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory (semester 5), which explicitly builds on it; Introduction to Programming (semester 1) precedes Algorithms & Data Structures (semester 5); Introduction to Data Science (semester 2) precedes Machine Learning (semester 3); Research Methods & Statistics (semester 2) precedes Statistics & Experimental Methods (semester 3) and Qualitative Research Methodology (semester 6). Formal prerequisites are all satisfied (Introduction to Programming before Algorithms & Data Structures) and every course sits in a semester in which it is offered. Personal & Professional Development is in year 1.
traceOverrides: analyses how film, photography, sound and digital media make ecological processes and environmental risk visible and shape how environmental problems are understood; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's media analysis and to the environmental side of Social and Environmental Impacts of the Digital Economy, although its focus is environmental representation

alternatives.label: Data, Algorithms and AI in Society: Technical Foundations with Social and Behavioural Perspectives
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum has twelve courses in programming, computer science, AI, data science and mathematics (Introduction to Programming, Mathematical Methods, Introduction to Data Science, Machine Learning, Neural Networks & Deep Learning, AI Ethics, Decision-making in AI, Optimization Methods in AI, Networks & Operating Systems, Database Management Systems, Algorithms & Data Structures and Probability & Statistics), three on research methods and statistics (Research Methods & Statistics, Statistics & Experimental Methods and Qualitative Research Methodology), and eight on the social, ethical and behavioural side (Ethics, Human Rights, Persuasive Communication, From T.V. to TikTok, Media Archaeology, Calling Bullshit, Marketing & Consumer Engagement and Behavioral Economics), plus Personal & Professional Development. The label names the technical majority first and the social and behavioural perspectives second; it does not claim a full computer-science or data-science degree.
alternatives.concept: A genuinely different route built on the programme's stated 'science behind GenAI, online safety, social media algorithms' and its data-analysis-for-social-questions direction rather than on its media, politics and ethics core. It gives technical depth that the closest match only samples: programming, databases, networks, algorithms, machine learning, neural networks and large language models, AI planning and optimization, and the mathematics and statistics beneath them, and it keeps the target's social questions through AI ethics, ethics, human rights, persuasion, social-media culture, misinformation, digital marketing and behavioural economics, with qualitative and quantitative methods. UCR has no independent research course in this field, so the programme has no equivalent of the target's thesis.
alternatives.distinctness: Alternative 1 builds the closest response to the target's interdisciplinary core from media, politics, sociology, ethics and business, with only four data and computing courses. Alternative 2 changes the organising priority to the technical object itself: the science behind generative AI and social-media algorithms and data analysis for social questions. This replaces Alternative 1's politics, sociology, business and creative-communication strands with twelve courses in programming, databases, networks, algorithms, machine learning, neural networks, AI decision-making, optimization, mathematics and statistics. The nine courses that differ from Alternative 1 (Mathematical Methods, Networks & Operating Systems, Database Management Systems, Neural Networks & Deep Learning, Probability & Statistics, Decision-making in AI, Optimization Methods in AI, Marketing & Consumer Engagement and Behavioral Economics) are consequences of that concept, not substitutions made to cross the 30-EC threshold.
progression: Introduction to Programming (semester 1) precedes Decision-making in AI, Networks & Operating Systems (semester 3), Database Management Systems (semester 4), Algorithms & Data Structures (semester 5) and Optimization Methods in AI (semester 6); Mathematical Methods (semester 2) precedes Probability & Statistics (semester 5) and Neural Networks & Deep Learning (semester 6); Introduction to Data Science (semester 1) precedes Machine Learning (semester 3); Research Methods & Statistics (semester 2) precedes Marketing & Consumer Engagement, Behavioral Economics (semester 6) and Statistics & Experimental Methods (semester 5). Formal prerequisites are satisfied and every course is offered in its semester. Personal & Professional Development is in year 1.
traceOverrides: examines the ethics of AI (fairness and bias, privacy, responsibility and accountability) together with the psychology of AI; it directly implements the ethical analysis of algorithmic and generative-AI systems that complements the technical courses in this programme

examines how television, film, podcasts and TikTok narratives shape social attitudes and everyday life, treating viral moments as cultural snapshots of contemporary values and anxieties; it directly engages the social-media and digital-culture content of the target's Digital Cultures, although from an American mainstream-media perspective

trains recognition of misinformation, fake news and cognitive biases, with a historical overview of misinformation in politics and society; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's online-harms and information-literacy themes, but is not specific to digital platforms

alternatives.label: Sustainability, Technology and Society: Environmental Science, Economics and Governance
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum has twelve courses in environment and sustainability (Sustainability Essentials I and II, Climate Change, Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy, Governance of Sustainability, Renewable System Design, R3, Research in a Sustainable Delta, Environmental Biogeochemistry, Earth Observation and Sustainable Farming & Innovation, plus Media & the Environment as a media-and-environment course), six in economics, business and digital transformation (Introduction to Economics, International Macroeconomics, Public Economics, Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations, Strategy & Digital Transformation and International Business & Governance), two in research methods and data (Research Methods & Statistics and Introduction to Data Science), and three in society, ethics and communication (Social Movements & Environmental Justice, Ethics and Communicating the Climate Crisis), plus Personal & Professional Development. Digital content is limited to data science, geospatial data and digital transformation, so the label names sustainability first and technology as one strand and does not claim a digital-society curriculum.
alternatives.concept: A question-led route built on the programme's question of how digital systems can be designed for environmental and social sustainability ('building a sustainable digital future', 'technology, people and the planet') and on its sustainability and post-growth-cities minor directions. It organises study around planetary limits and technology: sustainability essentials, climate change, life-cycle and circular-economy methods, energy and resource technologies, geospatial data, and sustainable food systems, together with the economics of growth and public policy, sustainability governance, environmental justice and degrowth perspectives, climate communication and responsible digital transformation and entrepreneurship. UCR has no urban-planning course available in the schedule (Spatial Planning is not offered in 2026-2029), so the post-growth-cities direction is represented through degrowth, economics and governance only, and the programme has no digital-systems design courses.
alternatives.distinctness: Alternative 1 organises study around the digital society itself (media, politics, sociology, ethics and data), and Alternative 2 around the technical science of algorithms and AI. Alternative 3 changes the organising question to sustainability: it drops the media-and-politics core and the technical computing core of the other two alternatives in favour of twelve environment and sustainability courses (Sustainability Essentials I and II, Climate Change, Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy, Governance of Sustainability, Renewable System Design, R3, Environmental Biogeochemistry, Earth Observation, Sustainable Farming & Innovation, Research in a Sustainable Delta and Media & the Environment), the economics of growth and public policy, and business and governance for responsible transformation. It shares only six courses with Alternative 1 and four with Alternative 2, and the courses that differ follow from the sustainability question rather than from threshold-filling.
progression: Sustainability Essentials I (semester 1) precedes Sustainability Essentials II (semester 2), Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy, Climate Change (semester 3), Earth Observation (semester 4), and Sustainability Essentials II precedes Renewable System Design and R3; Introduction to Economics (semester 1) and Research Methods & Statistics (semester 2) precede International Macroeconomics (semester 3) and Public Economics (semester 4); Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations (semester 1) precedes Strategy & Digital Transformation (semester 2) and International Business & Governance (semester 5). Formal prerequisites are satisfied and every course is offered in its semester. Personal & Professional Development is in year 1.

selection.assessment: Alternative 1 owns ten generator-eligible rows that describe the programme's own interdisciplinary core (5709, 5710, 5712, 5715, 5719, 5720, 5721, 5723, 5725, 5726): how digital technologies transform society, technology-people-planet, online safety and rights, designing digital systems for social good, digital politics and policy, digital ethics, digital business, creative digital communication, digital leadership and innovation and independent research. Nine further candidate directions were assessed. (1) Data, algorithms and AI (rows 5711, 5713, 5722, supported by 5717) passed evidence, coherence, distinctness and feasibility and became Alternative 2: the official programme description names the science behind generative AI and social-media algorithms, and UCR offers a deep computing, AI and data track; it shares 15 courses with Alternative 1 and differs in 9. (2) Sustainable digital futures and post-growth society (rows 5714, 5735, 5738, supported by 5710) passed the same gates and became Alternative 3: the programme description names a sustainable digital future, and UCR's environment and sustainability cluster is large; it shares 6 courses with Alternative 1 and 4 with Alternative 2. The remaining seven candidates are stopped by the maximum of three alternatives rather than by weak evidence or feasibility: Psychology and human decision-making (5733, 5737) and Arts, heritage and intellectual traditions (5727, 5731) and European studies, globalisation and development (5728, 5730) are each a coherent minor direction with substantial UCR course support, Law, policy and rights (5736), Gender and diversity (5729), Entrepreneurship (5734) and Sustainable healthcare (5732) are single-row formal minor directions with limited target-specific curricular evidence; none was rejected as a near-duplicate, and none was needed to reach three. Every included alternative passed the 30-EC pairwise floor and mechanical feasibility against the enriched workbook.

notes.text: The Bachelor Digital Society combines the sociological, ethical, technical, political and economic study of digitalisation, including digital cultures, digital politics and regulation, critical making and data skills. At UCR, students can approach digital society through fields such as media and communication, politics and law, sociology, ethics and AI ethics, business and economy of AI, and data science, programming and AI. These programmes therefore offer related perspectives rather than reproducing a full digital-society curriculum: UCR has no course on digital politics, digital regulation, virtual worlds or critical making.

The Bachelor Digital Society is organised as a fixed sequence of interdisciplinary core courses and skills in years 1 and 2, followed by a year-3 with 30 EC of open electives (a minor, study abroad, internship, literature exam or approved electives), a 17-EC thesis and two further research and controversies components. At UCR, comparable territory is distributed across separate single-discipline courses, and no course is an independent thesis, so the comparison treats the elective space and thesis as their own rows and places the standardized optional independent research element alongside the thesis.
